corrected_value.title: On the limits of language influences on numerical cognition – no inversion effects in three-digit number magnitude processing in adults
corrected_value.title_o: On the limits of language influences on numerical cognition – no inversion effects in three-digit number magnitude processing in adults

decisions.quote:
In particular, in a conceptual

replication attempt of the study by Bahnmueller et al. (2015), we employed the same three-

digit number comparison paradigm with Arabic digits in a comparable sample of German-

and English-speaking adults. However, instead of asking participants to indicate the larger of

two presented three-digit numbers we asked participants to indicate the smaller of two three-

digit numbers.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding (target 0) identify Bahnmueller et al. (2015) (DOI: 10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01216) as the primary original study re-tested in a conceptual replication using the same three-digit number comparison stimuli in a new sample with a marked task instruction.

decisions.quote:
Taken together, we successfully replicated main results reported by Bahnmueller et al.

(2015) showing that distance and compatibility effects in a three-digit number comparison

task generalize across marked and unmarked task instructions. Crucially, however, linguistic

markedness of task instructions did not seem to influence basic numerical processing as the

size of numerical effects was comparable between experiments using a marked compared to

an unmarked task instruction. In particular, results suggest that basic strategies in three-digit

number processing are rather robust against variations of the linguistic markedness of task

instructions.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding agree on 'successful'. The authors explicitly state an overall replication verdict that they successfully replicated the main results of Bahnmueller et al. (2015) (hundred distance, hundred-decade compatibility, and hundred-unit compatibility effects, as well as the absence of language-group differences between German and English speakers), with frequentist and Bayesian comparisons showing no significant differences in numerical effects between the two studies.

decisions.quote:
Here we

evaluate distance and compatibility effects in a three-digit number comparison task observed

in Bahnmueller et al. (2015) using a marked task instruction (i.e., ‘pick the smaller number’).

Moreover, we aimed at clarifying whether the markedness of task instruction influences

common numerical effects and especially componential processing as indexed by compatibility

effects. We instructed German- and English-speaking adults (N=52) to indicate the smaller

number in a three-digit number comparison task as opposed to indicating the larger number in

Bahnmueller et al. (2015).
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding agree on 'replication'. The paper collects new experimental data from a fresh sample of German- and English-speaking adults to conceptually replicate Bahnmueller et al. (2015) under a modified ('pick the smaller number') instruction; the accompanying re-analysis of the original dataset serves to compare the new sample's effects against the original experiment rather than constituting a standalone reproduction.
